newsitem.title: USA: U.S. gasoline demand seen rising, prices may not.
newsitem.headline: U.S. gasoline demand seen rising, prices may not.

text.p: U.S. gasoline and diesel fuel usage will climb to new heights during the peak "driving season" this year, but that may not translate into the kind of sharp price rise seen in 1996, analysts said.

Department of Energy forecasts released earlier this month estimated that April 1997 to January 1998 gasoline demand will sit comfortably above eight million barrels per day (bpd), compared with a 1996 average of 7.85 millin barrels.
"We have been expecting quite a strong outlook for U.S. demand," said Mohammed Abduljabbar, economist with Petroleum Finance Co in Washington, D.C.

DOE's Energy Information Administration sees second quarter demand increasing by 2.06 percent to 8.15 million bpd and third quarter demand to increased by 2.81 percent to 8.23 million bpd, or about 165,000 bpd and 225,000 bpd, respectively.
Overall 1997 demand should climb 2.27 percent, or 206,000 bpd to 8.027 million bpd, according to EIA's latest figures.
But analysts differed on the rate of increase from 1996 levels, since many believed the DOE underestimated consumption last year.

The DOE figures appeared to dramatically overestimate the 1995 imports of so-called blendstocks -- basically, gasoline that needs further processing -- but underestimated them in 1996, said Larry Goldstein, president of the Petroleum Industry Research Foundation Inc.
Goldstein said he was calling for overall gasoline consumption to increase by about 1.2 percent for 1997, or about 100,000 bpd.

"The gasoline near-term tightness still shows the risk of spike to the upside," Goldstein said, "but the overhang of crude will make it hard to hold the current price levels" during the peak summer driving season."

EIA's Dave Costello, who produced the agency's demand forecast, said that last year's late cold spell in the Northeast, which kept refinery production focused on heating oil, kept 1996 demand below expectations.
Costello said, "1996 stands out as a weak year," with EIA figures registering only a 0.8 percent increase from 1995 levels, well off prior calls for more than a two percent gain.
Gasoline futures prices in New York surged nearly 50 percent from early February to May last year as low stocks and the late refinery maintenance season delayed production.

"This year there is a longer transition between the winter and spring (demand seasons)," said Abduljabbar. "We will see a big jump in the production of gasoline. A spike in gasoline prices will be short-lived and earlier than last year, mainly because of the longer transition period." he added.
Refineries on the U.S. Gulf Coast, Northeast and Midwest entered maintenance earlier than normal this year, which will allow them to boost gasoline production as prices increase, analysts said.
Costello attributed the weaker-than-expected 1996 demand to the sharp jump in gasoline prices, which kept many motorists off the road.
However, Goldstein said price jumps typeically tend to push drivers away from premium gasoline grades and toward standard grades, but does not reduce overall U.S. mileage.
Improvements in the U.S. refining sector have made output more flexible, and as a result have boosted the level of blendstock imports from Europe, analysts said.
That flexibility resulted from new clean air standards that segmented the country into many different gasoline grades.
The steady growth in the U.S. economy and the low jobless figures will also keep gasoline demand on the uptrend, though a more direct effect is seen on diesel fuel.
"The trucking industry is really all of the diesel demand," said Ken Simonson, chief economist with the American Trucking Association in Arlington, Virginia.
"Gasoline depends much less on economic growth than diesel," Abduljabbar agreed, since trucking is tied more to sales and factory orders.
